claim: Two-component genetic systems can accumulate evolutionary novelty and diversify in the course of evolution.
source: How two-component genetic systems accumulate evolutionary novelty and diversify in the course of evolution is a fundamental problem in evolutionary systems biology.
evidence: This is a general statement about two-component genetic systems presented in the introduction as context for the study.

claim: Self-incompatibility in Brassicaceae is a spectacular example of a diversified allelic series in which numerous highly diverged receptor-ligand combinations are segregating in natural populations.
source: In the Brassicaceae, self-incompatibility (SI) is a spectacular example of a diversified allelic series in which numerous highly diverged receptor-ligand combinations are segregating in natural populations.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge about the SI system in Brassicaceae.

claim: Two allelic variants segregating as distinct receptor-ligand combinations diverged through an asymmetrical process whereby one variant has retained the same recognition specificity as their putative ancestor, while the other has functionally diverged.
source: Using in planta ancestral protein reconstruction, we demonstrate that two allelic variants segregating as distinct receptor-ligand combinations diverged through an asymmetrical process whereby one variant has retained the same recognition specificity as their (now extinct) putative ancestor, while the other has functionally diverged and now represents a novel specificity no longer recognized by the ancestor.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data from ancestral protein reconstruction and functional assays.

claim: Qualitative rather than quantitative changes of the interaction are an important source of evolutionary novelty in this highly diversified receptor-ligand system.
source: Examination of the structural determinants of the shift in binding specificity suggests that qualitative rather than quantitative changes of the interaction are an important source of evolutionary novelty in this highly diversified receptor-ligand system.
evidence: This conclusion is based on structural modeling analysis of the receptor-ligand complexes.

claim: Many cellular processes rely on interactions between molecular partners rather than on the action of individual components in isolation.
source: A major challenge toward this goal is that many cellular processes rely on interactions between molecular partners (protein-protein interactions or regulatory interactions between for example transcription factors and their binding sites; Boyle et al., 2017; Courtier-Orgogozo et al., 2019) rather than on the action of individual components in isolation.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: A general understanding of how the diversification of protein-protein or regulatory interaction networks led to the emergence of new biological functions in distinct lineages is crucially lacking.
source: At present, the overall structure of protein-protein or regulatory interaction networks is just starting to be understood at the genome level in a handful of model organisms, and a general understanding of how the diversification of these networks led to the emergence of new biological functions in distinct lineages is crucially lacking (Nooren and Thornton, 2003; Andreani and Guerois, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: In two-component genetic systems, specificity of the interaction can be very tight such as for example in receptor-ligand interactions or bacterial toxin-antitoxin systems.
source: In two-component genetic systems, specificity of the interaction can be very tight such as for example in receptor-ligand interactions (Laub and Goulian, 2007) or bacterial toxin-antitoxin systems (Aakre et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: The emergence of novel traits in two-component systems involves evolutionary modification of the interacting partners, leading to potential disruption of the interaction or to detrimental cross-talk, at least transiently.
source: In these systems, the emergence of novel traits involves evolutionary modification of the interacting partners, leading to potential disruption of the interaction or to detrimental cross-talk, at least transiently (Plach et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to other scholarly work.

claim: Two main scenarios have been proposed for the functional nature of the evolutionary intermediate in two-component systems.
source: Two main scenarios have been proposed (Aakre et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to other scholarly work.

claim: The first scenario posits that a functional change results from introduction of a mutation that first modifies one of the two partners, initially disrupting the functional interaction and leading to a non-functional intermediate.
source: The first scenario posits that a functional change results from introduction of a mutation that first modifies one of the two partners, initially disrupting the functional interaction and leading to a non-functional intermediate.
evidence: This is a description of a theoretical scenario from the literature.

claim: An alternative scenario is that the first mutation may broaden rather than inactivate specificity of one of the two interacting partners, transiently releasing constraint on the other before specificity of the first partner becomes restricted again.
source: An alternative scenario though, is that the first mutation may broaden rather than inactivate specificity of one of the two interacting partners, transiently releasing constraint on the other before specificity of the first partner becomes restricted again, thus maintaining functionality of the system all along the process.
evidence: This is a description of a theoretical scenario from the literature.

claim: Distinguishing between the two scenarios of evolutionary intermediates requires functional characterization of the ancestral evolutionary intermediates.
source: Distinguishing between these two scenarios requires functional characterization of the ancestral evolutionary intermediates, which has been achieved in a very limited number of biological cases such as bacterial toxin-antitoxin systems (Aakre et al., 2015), acquisition of cortisol specificity of the mammalian glucocorticoid receptor (Bridgham et al., 2009) or mammalian retinoic acid receptors (Gutierrez-Mazariegos et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: The scenario of a promiscuous intermediate seems to have received better support in previous studies.
source: The scenario of a promiscuous intermediate seems to have received better support, but whether this is a truly general pattern remains to be determined.
evidence: This is an inference based on the literature review presented.

claim: Detailed population genetic models taking into account how natural selection is acting on variants of the two genes given their specific biological function are lacking for most genetic systems.
source: A major limitation is that detailed population genetic models taking into account how natural selection is acting on variants of the two genes given their specific biological function are lacking for most genetic systems (Aakre et al., 2015; Aharoni et al., 2005; Bloom and Arnold, 2009; Bridgham et al., 2009; Matsumura and Ellington, 2001; Matton et al., 2000; Sayou et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: Self-incompatibility in flowering plants is a prime biological system to investigate how functional diversification can proceed between two molecular partners over the course of evolution.
source: Self-incompatibility (SI) in flowering plants is a prime biological system to investigate how functional diversification can proceed between two molecular partners over the course of evolution.
evidence: This is a statement about the suitability of the SI system for studying evolutionary processes.

claim: SI has evolved as a strategy to prevent selfing and enforce outcrossing, thereby avoiding the deleterious effects of inbreeding depression.
source: SI has evolved as a strategy to prevent selfing and enforce outcrossing, thereby avoiding the deleterious effects of inbreeding depression (Nettancourt, 1977; Kitashiba and Nasrallah, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: In Brassicaceae, SI is genetically controlled by a single multiallelic non-recombining locus called the S-locus.
source: In Brassicaceae, SI is genetically controlled by a single multiallelic non-recombining locus called the S-locus (Nettancourt, 1977).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to other scholarly work.

claim: The S-locus encodes two highly polymorphic self-recognition determinant proteins: the female cell-surface 'receptor' S-LOCUS RECEPTOR KINASE (SRK) and the male 'ligand' S-LOCUS CYSTEIN RICH PROTEIN (SCR).
source: This locus encodes two highly polymorphic self-recognition determinant proteins: the female cell-surface 'receptor' S-LOCUS RECEPTOR KINASE (SRK) is expressed in stigmatic papillae cells (Takasaki et al., 2000) and the male 'ligand' S-LOCUS CYSTEIN RICH PROTEIN (SCR) is displayed at the pollen surface (Schopfer et al., 1999; Takasaki et al., 2000; Takayama et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: The SI response consists in pollen rejection by the pistil and is induced by allele-specific interaction between the SRK and SCR proteins when encoded by the same haplotype.
source: The SI response consists in pollen rejection by the pistil and is induced by allele-specific interaction between the SRK and SCR proteins when encoded by the same haplotype (S-haplotype, Kachroo et al., 2001; Nasrallah and Nasrallah, 1993; Takayama et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: SRK and SCR proteins exhibit a high degree of sequence variability and a large number of these highly diverged allelic variants segregate in natural populations of SI species.
source: These two interacting proteins exhibit a high degree of sequence variability and a large number of these highly diverged allelic variants segregate in natural populations of SI species (several dozens to nearly two hundred, Busch et al., 2014; Castric and Vekemans, 2004; Lawrence, 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: The large allelic diversity of receptor-ligand combinations must have arisen through repeated diversification events, but the molecular process and evolutionary scenario involved in the diversification of an ancestral haplotype into distinct descendant specificities are still unresolved.
source: This large allelic diversity of receptor-ligand combinations must have arisen through repeated diversification events, but the molecular process and evolutionary scenario involved in the diversification of an ancestral haplotype into distinct descendant specificities are still unresolved.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Three evolutionary scenarios for emergence of new self-incompatibility specificities have been proposed.
source: Three evolutionary scenarios for emergence of new self-incompatibility specificities have been proposed so far (Charlesworth et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to other scholarly work.

claim: The 'compensatory mutation' scenario posits that diversification proceeds through self-compatible intermediates following transient disruption of the receptor-ligand interaction.
source: The 'compensatory mutation' scenario posits that diversification proceeds through self-compatible intermediates that is following transient disruption of the receptor-ligand interaction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Gervais et al., 2011; Uyenoyama et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work and reference to a figure.

claim: Population genetic analysis confirmed that S-allele diversification is possible through the compensatory mutation scenario, but only under some combinations of model parameters.
source: Population genetic analysis confirmed that S-allele diversification is indeed possible through this scenario, but only under some combinations of model parameters (high inbreeding depression, high rate of self-pollination and low number of co-segregating S-alleles, Gervais et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to other scholarly work.

claim: Under restrictive conditions, the ancestral recognition specificity can be maintained in the long run along with the derived specificity, effectively resulting in allelic diversification.
source: Under these restrictive conditions, the ancestral recognition specificity can be maintained in the long run along with the derived specificity, effectively resulting in allelic diversification.
evidence: This is an inference based on population genetic analysis cited in the text.

claim: Chookajorn et al. (2004) proposed that diversification results from the progressive reinforcement of SRK/SCR recognition capacity among slight functional variants that might segregate within the population.
source: A second scenario was presented by Chookajorn et al. (2004), who proposed that diversification results from the progressive reinforcement of SRK/SCR recognition capacity among slight functional variants of SCR and SRK that might segregate within the population.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to other scholarly work.

claim: The progressive reinforcement process may result in the production of two descendant allelic specificities that are both functionally distinct from their ancestor.
source: However, the progressive reinforcement process proposed by this model may rather result in the production of two descendant allelic specificities that are both functionally distinct from their ancestor (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of the model proposed by Chookajorn et al.

claim: A third scenario proposed by Matton et al. (1999) involves a dual-specificity intermediate.
source: A third scenario was proposed by Matton et al. (1999) and involves a dual-specificity intermediate (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to other scholarly work.

claim: The dual-specificity scenario was criticized on population genetics grounds because such a dual-specificity haplotype would recognize and reject more potential mates for reproduction than its progenitor haplotype resulting in lower reproductive success.
source: This scenario was criticized on population genetics grounds because such a dual-specificity haplotype would recognize and reject more potential mates for reproduction than its progenitor haplotype resulting in lower reproductive success, and should therefore be disfavoured by natural selection and quickly eliminated from the populations (Charlesworth, 2000; Uyenoyama and Newbigin, 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: A main unanswered question is whether functional specificities remain stable over time or are subject to frequent turnover.
source: A main unanswered question is whether functional specificities remain stable over time or are subject to frequent turnover.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Under a large portion of the parameter space, the introduced self-compatible intermediate is predicted to exclude its functional ancestor from the population.
source: Detailed theoretical analysis of the model of Gervais et al. (2011) showed that under a large portion of the parameter space, the introduced self-compatible intermediate is predicted to exclude its functional ancestor from the population.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to other scholarly work.

claim: Secondary introduction of the compensatory mutation effectively results in turnover of recognition specificities along allelic lines rather than in diversification per se.
source: Secondary introduction of the compensatory mutation then effectively results in turnover of recognition specificities along allelic lines rather than in diversification per se.
evidence: This is an inference based on the theoretical analysis cited.

claim: A turnover of recognition specificities may be expected along each allelic lineage, rather than their long-term maintenance over evolutionary times.
source: A turnover of recognition specificities may therefore be expected along each allelic lineage, rather than their long-term maintenance over evolutionary times.
evidence: This is an inference based on the theoretical analysis discussed.

claim: An essential limitation in the field is the crucial absence of direct experimental approaches.
source: Overall, while the large allelic diversity at the S-locus is one of the most striking features of this system, the evolutionary scenario and molecular route by which new S-alleles arise remain largely unknown. An essential limitation in the field is the crucial absence of direct experimental approaches.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field.

claim: Previous work identified a pair of S-haplotypes (S03 and S28) with high phylogenetic proximity based on a fragment of the SRK gene.
source: Although most S-haplotypes in A. halleri are typically so highly diverged that even sequence alignment can be challenging, previous work identified a pair of S-haplotypes (S03 and S28) with high phylogenetic proximity based on a fragment of the SRK gene (Castric et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to other scholarly work.

claim: The putative last common ancestor of SRK03 and SRK28 was reconstructed, resurrected and phenotypically characterized into A. thaliana.
source: We took this opportunity to reconstruct, resurrect and phenotypically characterize their putative last common ancestral receptor SRKa ('a' for ancestor, Figure 1) into A. thaliana, which has previously been established as a model plant for mechanistic studies of SI (Nasrallah et al., 2002; Tsuchimatsu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: A. thaliana has previously been established as a model plant for mechanistic studies of SI.
source: We took this opportunity to reconstruct, resurrect and phenotypically characterize their putative last common ancestral receptor SRKa ('a' for ancestor, Figure 1) into A. thaliana, which has previously been established as a model plant for mechanistic studies of SI (Nasrallah et al., 2002; Tsuchimatsu et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: Four different versions of SRKa were defined due to inference uncertainty at two amino acid positions.
source: Four different versions of SRKa were defined due to inference uncertainty at two aa positions.
evidence: This is stated in the figure caption and is based on the phylogenetic reconstruction.

claim: SRK03 and SRK28 sequences were cloned from A. halleri DNA BAC clones, whereas SRKa sequences were obtained by gene synthesis.
source: SRK03 and SRK28 sequences were cloned from A. halleri DNA BAC clones, whereas SRKa sequences were obtained by gene synthesis.
evidence: This is a description of the methods used in the study.

claim: The self-compatible model plant A. thaliana can mount a functional self-incompatibility response upon introduction of the S-locus genes SCR and SRK.
source: It was previously shown that the self-compatible model plant A. thaliana can mount a functional self-incompatibility response upon introduction of the S-locus genes SCR and SRK (Boggs et al., 2009; Durand et al., 2014; Nasrallah et al., 2002) but it is unclear whether transfer is possible for all SCR and SRK variants.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: It is unclear whether transfer of SI function to A. thaliana is possible for all SCR and SRK variants.
source: It was previously shown that the self-compatible model plant A. thaliana can mount a functional self-incompatibility response upon introduction of the S-locus genes SCR and SRK (Boggs et al., 2009; Durand et al., 2014; Nasrallah et al., 2002) but it is unclear whether transfer is possible for all SCR and SRK variants.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: AhSRK03 and AhSRK28 promoters are active in transformed A. thaliana lines.
source: We first assessed the activity of AhSRK03 and AhSRK28 promoters in transformed A. thaliana lines (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), which enabled us to identify the temporal window of SRK expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: A proper SI response was successfully transferred in transformed A. thaliana lines for each of the SRK receptors (SRK03 and SRK28).
source: Then, we used A. halleri pollen carrying either the S03 or S28 male determinant to validate that a proper SI response was indeed successfully transferred in transformed A. thaliana lines for each of our SRK receptors, and that this response was strictly specific toward either of their cognate ligand (two replicate transgenic lines for SRK03 and SRK28 each, Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: The SI response in transformed A. thaliana lines was strictly specific toward the cognate ligand.
source: Then, we used A. halleri pollen carrying either the S03 or S28 male determinant to validate that a proper SI response was indeed successfully transferred in transformed A. thaliana lines for each of our SRK receptors, and that this response was strictly specific toward either of their cognate ligand (two replicate transgenic lines for SRK03 and SRK28 each, Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: A robust self-incompatibility reaction is observed between cognate alleles, whereas a compatible reaction is observed between non-cognate alleles.
source: A robust self-incompatibility reaction is observed between cognate alleles, whereas a compatible reaction is observed between non-cognate alleles.
evidence: This is stated in the figure caption and supported by the microscopy images.

claim: Abundant germination of pollen tubes occurred in crosses involving non-cognate SRK and SCR proteins.
source: Abundant germination of pollen tubes occurred in crosses involving non-cognate SRK and SCR proteins, whereas crosses involving proteins from the same S-haplotype induced inhibition of pollen germination, which is characteristic of an incompatible response.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from pollination assays.

claim: Crosses involving proteins from the same S-haplotype induced inhibition of pollen germination, which is characteristic of an incompatible response.
source: Abundant germination of pollen tubes occurred in crosses involving non-cognate SRK and SCR proteins, whereas crosses involving proteins from the same S-haplotype induced inhibition of pollen germination, which is characteristic of an incompatible response.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from pollination assays.

claim: Incompatible responses are characterized by less than 10 germinated pollen tubes whereas compatible crosses induced significant pollen germination, with more than 50 pollen tubes per stigma.
source: Incompatible responses are characterized by less than 10 germinated pollen tubes whereas compatible crosses induced significant pollen germination, with more than 50 pollen tubes per stigma.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from pollination assays.

claim: Cross-species pollinations of A. thaliana with A. halleri pollen can induce robust SI reactions.
source: This shows that cross-species pollinations of A. thaliana with A. halleri pollen can induce robust SI reactions, and also that S03 and S28 have distinct recognition specificities, despite their close phylogenetic proximity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data from pollination assays.

claim: S03 and S28 have distinct recognition specificities, despite their close phylogenetic proximity.
source: This shows that cross-species pollinations of A. thaliana with A. halleri pollen can induce robust SI reactions, and also that S03 and S28 have distinct recognition specificities, despite their close phylogenetic proximity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data from pollination assays.

claim: A phylogenetic approach was used to reconstruct the sequence of the most recent common ancestor of SRK03 and SRK28.
source: We then used a phylogenetic approach to reconstruct the sequence of the most recent common ancestor of SRK03 and SRK28 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a description of the methods used in the study.

claim: The best fitting codon-based models implemented in PAML were used to reconstruct the most likely ancestral amino acid sequence (SRKa).
source: Based on a set of closely related SRK sequences from Arabidopsis and Capsella, we used the best fitting codon-based models implemented in PAML (Yang, 2007) to reconstruct the most likely ancestral amino acid sequence (SRKa).
evidence: This is a description of the methods used in the study.

claim: For the vast majority of the 56 amino acid residues where SRK03 and SRK28 differ, the ancestral reconstruction had high posterior probability (>0.95).
source: For the vast majority of the 56 amino acid residues where SRK03 and SRK28 differ (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), the ancestral reconstruction had high posterior probability (>0.95), but was more uncertain at four positions (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic reconstruction analysis.

claim: The ancestral reconstruction was more uncertain at four positions.
source: For the vast majority of the 56 amino acid residues where SRK03 and SRK28 differ (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), the ancestral reconstruction had high posterior probability (>0.95), but was more uncertain at four positions (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic reconstruction analysis.

claim: Two of the uncertain sites were close (208) or within (305) hyper variable regions known to be functionally important.
source: Two of these sites were close (208) or within (305) hyper variable regions known to be functionally important (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Kusaba et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to other scholarly work.

claim: Three additional ancestral sequences were generated and tested to take uncertainty into account: SRKaIG, SRKaMA and SRKaMG.
source: To take uncertainty into account and evaluate the impact of variation at these two individual sites, three additional ancestral sequences were generated and tested: SRKaIG, SRKaMA and SRKaMG.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: A total of 28 different fixed homozygote single-copy transformed Arabidopsis lines were obtained.
source: For each of these constructs, we obtained several replicate transgenic lines, resulting in a total of 28 different fixed homozygote single-copy transformed Arabidopsis lines (8 SRKaIA lines; 7 SRKaIG lines; 7 SRKaMA lines and 6 SRKaMG lines).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental results.

claim: Five lines showed very low levels of SRKa transcripts in pistils and were excluded from further analysis.
source: Five lines showed very low levels of SRKa transcripts in pistils (Figure 3—figure supplement 3; possibly due to positional effects as is common in transgenic constructs) and were thus excluded from further analysis, leaving 23 transgenic lines for testing.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: With a single exception, S28 pollen induced no consistent SI rejection in any of the lines expressing the different versions of the ancestral receptor.
source: With a single exception (line p03_SRKaMA_k03_2), S28 pollen induced no consistent SI rejection in any of the lines expressing the different versions of the ancestral receptor, and was indistinguishable from the compatible control (C24, Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: SCR03 pollen induced robust incompatibility reactions in the vast majority (12 of 14) of the lines with amino acid I at position 208 (SRKaIA and SRKaIG).
source: In stark contrast, SCR03 pollen induced robust incompatibility reactions in the vast majority (12 of 14) of the lines with amino acid I at position 208 (SRKaIA and SRKaIG, Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: The S03 haplotype has retained the ancestral recognition specificity largely unaltered, while the S28 haplotype underwent substantial modification and represents a novel recognition specificity.
source: Hence, we conclude that the S03 haplotype has retained the ancestral recognition specificity largely unaltered, while the S28 haplotype underwent substantial modification and represents a novel recognition specificity, leading to functional diversification.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data from pollination assays.

claim: The incompatibility reactions involving different ancestral SRK S-domain sequences were largely independent of the sequence context into which they were introduced.
source: The incompatibility reactions involving our different ancestral SRK S-domain sequences were largely independent of the sequence context into which we introduced them (Figure 3, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: The amino acid present at position 305 of the reconstructed sequence had no effect on the response.
source: Similarly, the amino acid present at position 305 of the reconstructed sequence had no effect on the response: lines with either A or G produced rejection reactions equally.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from pollination assays.

claim: Only four of the lines with amino acid M at position 208 (SRKaMA and SRKaMG) displayed incompatibility reactions, and these were weak.
source: In contrast, only four of the lines with amino acid M at position 208 (SRKaMA and SRKaMG) displayed incompatibility reactions, and these were weak (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: The single change from the ancestral Isoleucine amino acid (I) at position 208 to Methionine (M) seems to be sufficient to almost fully inactivate the ancestral receptor's ability to recognise SCR03.
source: Hence, the single change, from the ancestral Isoleucine amino acid (I) at position 208 to Methionine (M), seems to be sufficient to almost fully inactivate the ancestral receptor's ability to recognise SCR03.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data from pollination assays.

claim: The structural model of the interaction complex formed by SCR and SRK was used to compare cognate and non cognate complexes.
source: We used the structural model of the interaction complex formed by SCR and SRK (Ma et al., 2016) to compare cognate and non cognate complexes in terms of number and nature of atomic contacts and predict how the ancestral receptor is expected to interact with either SCR03 or SCR28.
evidence: This is a description of the methods used in the study.

claim: SCR binding induces homodimerization of the extracellular domain of SRK (eSRK), forming eSRK:SCR heterotetramers composed of two SCR molecules bound to two SRK molecules.
source: As previously demonstrated by Ma et al. (2016), SCR binding induces homodimerization of the extracellular domain of SRK (eSRK, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), forming eSRK:SCR heterotetramers composed of two SCR molecules bound to two SRK molecules (Ma et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to other scholarly work.

claim: The switch in recognition specificity occurred along the branch leading to SRK28, and therefore must involve some of the 29 amino acid differences along this branch.
source: The switch in recognition specificity occurred along the branch leading to SRK28, and therefore must involve some of the 29 amino acid differences along this branch.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic analysis and experimental results.

claim: The 31 amino acid differences that accumulated along the branch leading to SRK03 have not fully altered the recognition specificity.
source: In contrast, the 31 amino acid differences that accumulated along the branch leading to SRK03 have not fully altered the recognition specificity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic analysis and experimental results.

claim: There is a slightly higher number of atomic contacts between the SCR and SRK molecules in the SRK03-SCR03 cognate complex (1543 contacts) than in the SRK28-SCR28 cognate complex (1395 contacts).
source: Overall, we find a slightly higher number of atomic contacts between the SCR and SRK molecules in the SRK03-SCR03 cognate complex (1543 contacts over 91 and 62 distinct SRK and SCR amino acids respectively) than in the SRK28-SCR28 cognate complex (1395 contacts over 89 and 57 distinct SRK and SCR amino acids respectively, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by structural modeling analysis.

claim: In both cases the interaction interface was mostly concentrated around the three 'hypervariable' portions of the SRK protein.
source: As already noted by Ma et al. (2016) in Brassica, and in line with the distribution of positively selected sites along the sequence (Castric and Vekemans, 2007), in both cases the interaction interface was mostly concentrated around the three 'hypervariable' portions of the SRK protein (Figure 4).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work and structural modeling analysis.

claim: The non-cognate complexes did not differ substantially from the cognate complexes on the basis of their total number of atomic contacts.
source: Contrary to our expectation, however, the non-cognate complexes did not differ substantially from the cognate complexes on the basis of their total number of atomic contacts (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by structural modeling analysis.

claim: The SRK03/SCR28 and SRK28/SCR03 non-cognate complexes were predicted to establish a total of 1546 and 1328 contacts, respectively.
source: Specifically, the SRK03/SCR28 and SRK28/SCR03 non-cognate complexes were predicted to establish a total of 1546 and 1328 contacts, respectively, between atoms of their SCR and SRK molecules, very close to the 1543 and 1395 predicted contacts for the SRK03/SCR03 and SRK28/SCR28 cognate complexes (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by structural modeling analysis.

claim: The non-cognate complexes were not characterized by any obvious steric clashes that would prevent the proper docking of SCR and SRK.
source: They were also not characterized by any obvious steric clashes that would prevent the proper docking of SCR and SRK.
evidence: This is supported by structural modeling analysis.

claim: The overall stability of the complex does not seem to be the primary determinant of recognition specificity.
source: Hence, the overall stability of the complex does not seem to be the primary determinant of recognition specificity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural modeling analysis.

claim: The specificity of the interaction must be a function of some qualitative features rather than of the quantitative strength of the interaction.
source: Consequently, the specificity of the interaction must be a function of some qualitative features rather than of the quantitative strength of the interaction.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural modeling analysis.

claim: Six amino acid positions of the eSRK protein displayed important differences in terms of contacts they establish with SCR in the cognate vs. the non-cognate complexes.
source: While the majority of amino acids retained unchanged atomic contacts in cognate vs. non-cognate interactions, using a 5% threshold we identified six amino acid positions of the eSRK protein that displayed important differences in terms of contacts they establish with SCR in the cognate vs. the non-cognate complexes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, C, E and F).
evidence: This is supported by structural modeling analysis.

claim: Four amino acid positions (S201, R220, R279, W296) displayed very contrasted interactions in the S03 vs. the S28 complexes.
source: Four of these amino acid positions also displayed very contrasted interactions in the S03 vs. the S28 complexes (residues S201, R220, R279, W296, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and D).
evidence: This is supported by structural modeling analysis.

claim: The R residue at position 279 of SRK establishes three times more contacts with SCR in the SRK03/SCR03 than in the SRK28/SCR28 complex.
source: For instance, the R residue at position 279 of SRK establishes three times more contacts with SCR in the SRK03/SCR03 than in the SRK28/SCR28 complex (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by structural modeling analysis.

claim: Residues S201, R220, R279, and W296 are prime candidates for the determination of binding specificity.
source: These four residues are therefore prime candidates for the determination of binding specificity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural modeling analysis.

claim: Three of the six amino acids were identical between SRK03 and SRK28, and yet interacted in sharply different ways with their respective SCR ligands.
source: Intriguingly, three of the six amino acids were identical between SRK03 and SRK28, and yet interacted in sharply different ways with their respective SCR ligands.
evidence: This is supported by structural modeling analysis.

claim: Residues W296 and R279 established three to four times more contacts in the S03 than in the S28 complex, while being identical between the SRK03 and SRK28 sequences.
source: For instance, while identical between the SRK03 and SRK28 sequences, residues W296 and R279 established three to four times more contacts in the S03 than in the S28 complex, and the R220 residue is involved in twice as many contacts in the S28 than in the S03 complex (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by structural modeling analysis.

claim: The R220 residue is involved in twice as many contacts in the S28 than in the S03 complex, while being identical between the SRK03 and SRK28 sequences.
source: For instance, while identical between the SRK03 and SRK28 sequences, residues W296 and R279 established three to four times more contacts in the S03 than in the S28 complex, and the R220 residue is involved in twice as many contacts in the S28 than in the S03 complex (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by structural modeling analysis.

claim: Involvement of these residues in the activity of the complex is mediated by substitutions at other positions along the protein sequence, for instance by displacing them spatially.
source: This suggests that involvement of these residues in the activity of the complex is mediated by substitutions at other positions along the protein sequence, for instance by displacing them spatially (Figure 5).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural modeling analysis.

claim: When complexed with SCR03, 46 SRKaIA interacting pairs of amino acids were identical with SRK03, whereas only 24 were identical with SRK28.
source: When complexed with SCR03, 46 SRKaIA interacting pairs of amino acids were identical with SRK03, whereas only 24 were identical with SRK28.
evidence: This is supported by structural modeling analysis.

claim: When complexed with SCR28, 37 SRKaIA interacting pairs of amino acid residues were identical with SRK03, but only 18 were identical with SRK28.
source: Similarly, when complexed with SCR28, 37 SRKaIA interacting pairs of amino acid residues were identical with SRK03, but only 18 were identical with SRK28 (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by structural modeling analysis.

claim: There is no quantitative difference in how strongly SRK03 and SRK28 bind SCR03 and SCR28.
source: Hence, even though there is no quantitative difference in how strongly SRK03 and SRK28 bind SCR03 and SCR28 (Supplementary file 1), the amino acids that come into contact in the two complexes are not identical, and the contacts established by SRKaIA with SCR qualitatively resemble more those established by SRK03 than those established by SRK28.
evidence: This is supported by structural modeling analysis.

claim: The amino acids that come into contact in the two complexes are not identical.
source: Hence, even though there is no quantitative difference in how strongly SRK03 and SRK28 bind SCR03 and SCR28 (Supplementary file 1), the amino acids that come into contact in the two complexes are not identical, and the contacts established by SRKaIA with SCR qualitatively resemble more those established by SRK03 than those established by SRK28.
evidence: This is supported by structural modeling analysis.

claim: The contacts established by SRKaIA with SCR qualitatively resemble more those established by SRK03 than those established by SRK28.
source: Hence, even though there is no quantitative difference in how strongly SRK03 and SRK28 bind SCR03 and SCR28 (Supplementary file 1), the amino acids that come into contact in the two complexes are not identical, and the contacts established by SRKaIA with SCR qualitatively resemble more those established by SRK03 than those established by SRK28.
evidence: This is supported by structural modeling analysis.

claim: Asymmetrical diversification of the ancestor into the phenotypically distinct S03 and S28 specificities is associated with structural changes of the SRK receptor and the way it interacts with its SCR ligand.
source: Overall, asymmetrical diversification of the ancestor into the phenotypically distinct S03 and S28 specificities is therefore associated with structural changes of the SRK receptor and the way it interacts with its SCR ligand.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural modeling analysis and experimental results.

claim: Despite similar levels of overall sequence divergence between SRKa and either SRK03 or SRK28, the binding properties of SRK03 have remained similar to those of SRKaIA, while the way SRK28 is predicted to interact with the SCR ligand has diverged from its ancestral state.
source: Despite similar levels of overall sequence divergence between SRKa and either SRK03 or SRK28, the binding properties of SRK03 have remained similar to those of SRKaIA, while the way SRK28 is predicted to interact with the SCR ligand has diverged from its ancestral state, consistent with the phenotypic switch that has occurred along this lineage.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural modeling analysis and experimental results.

claim: Ancestral resurrection approaches have been used to decipher evolutionary processes in a number of biological systems including enzymes, visual pigments, and transcription factors.
source: Ancestral resurrection approaches have been used to decipher evolutionary processes in a number of biological systems including enzymes (Starr et al., 2017; Tufts et al., 2015), visual pigments (Chang et al., 2002) or transcription factors (Pougach et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: An essential limitation in ancestral resurrection studies is that the ancestral protein function is typically determined in vitro, strongly limiting biological realism of the reconstructed function.
source: However, an essential limitation in these studies is that the ancestral protein function is typically determined in vitro, strongly limiting biological realism of the reconstructed function.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of previous studies.

claim: A single study involved a comparable in vivo ancestral resurrection approach in a higher organism, in the context of functional evolution of the alcohol dehydrogenase protein (ADH) in Drosophila lineages.
source: To our knowledge, a single study involved a comparable in vivo ancestral resurrection approach in a higher organism, in the context of functional evolution of the alcohol dehydrogenase protein (ADH) in Drosophila lineages (Siddiq et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to other scholarly work.

claim: Whole organism studies are biologically most relevant, as they allow a focus on integrated phenotypes rather than on highly reductionist phenotypes.
source: Such whole organism studies are biologically most relevant, as they allow a focus on integrated phenotypes (here the self-incompatibility reaction, which has a strong and direct link with organismal fitness) rather than on highly reductionist phenotypes (such as in vitro assays of protein activity).
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of whole organism studies.

claim: Functional diversification of receptor-ligand interactions is a common process that takes place over long evolutionary times.
source: Functional diversification of receptor-ligand interactions is a common process that takes place over long evolutionary times.
evidence: This is a general statement about receptor-ligand interactions.

claim: Little is known about how diversification happens in nature, both in terms of whether some evolutionary pathways are preferentially followed over others and in terms of the molecular modifications involved.
source: However, in most cases we remain far from a predictive understanding of how the specific evolutionary forces imposed on a given interacting pair of proteins at the molecular level translate into a given process of functional diversification. As a result, little is known about how diversification happens in nature, both in terms of whether some evolutionary pathways are preferentially followed over others and in terms of the molecular modifications involved.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Diversification of two S-alleles from their putative common ancestor proceeded through asymmetrical functional divergence, with one allele having largely retained its ancestral specificity and the other one having acquired a novel recognition specificity that was previously absent.
source: Here, we show that diversification of two S-alleles from their putative common ancestor proceeded through asymmetrical functional divergence, with one allele having largely retained its ancestral specificity and the other one having acquired a novel recognition specificity that was previously absent.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: The results are compatible with the model of SI specificity diversification by compensatory mutation of Gervais et al. (2011) and one version of the progressive reinforcement model of Chookajorn et al. (2004).
source: Overall, our results are thus compatible with the model of SI specificity diversification by compensatory mutation of Gervais et al. (2011) and one version (i.e. with maintenance of the ancestral specificity) of the progressive reinforcement model of Chookajorn et al. (2004).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results and comparison with theoretical models.

claim: The results do not allow to discriminate between the compensatory mutation model and the progressive reinforcement model, that is to determine whether a transient loss of self-recognition is required.
source: However, they do not allow to discriminate between these two models, that is to determine whether a transient loss of self-recognition is required (Uyenoyama et al., 2001; Gervais et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the study.

claim: The model of promiscuous dual-specificity intermediates can be rejected.
source: In contrast, the model of promiscuous dual-specificity intermediates (Matton et al., 1999; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) can be rejected, because Uyenoyama and Newbigin (2000) have shown that a dual-specificity haplotype can be maintained in the population only in the absence of the ancestral specificity, while we show here that the ancestral specificity (S03) remained present.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results and comparison with theoretical models.

claim: The progressive reinforcement model with replacement of the ancestral specificity by two functionally diverged specificities can be rejected.
source: Similarly, the progressive reinforcement model with replacement of the ancestral specificity by two functionally diverged specificities can be rejected (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results and comparison with theoretical models.

claim: Models of SI evolution suggested that turnover of recognition specificities may be common over evolutionary times.
source: Models of SI evolution suggested that turnover of recognition specificities may be common over evolutionary times (Gervais et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to other scholarly work.

claim: The observation that the ancestral SRKaIA recognition specificity was stably maintained along the SRK03 lineage demonstrates that no turnover event occurred over a substantial period of time.
source: The observation that the ancestral SRKaIA recognition specificity was stably maintained along the SRK03 lineage demonstrates that no turnover event occurred over a substantial period of time (i.e. since S03 and S28 started to diverge from one another, ca. a few million years ago).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results.

claim: The long-term maintenance of S-haplotype specificities was previously suggested by the comparison of certain A. halleri and A. lyrata S-lineages with their A. thaliana orthologs.
source: The long-term maintenance of S-haplotype specificities was previously suggested by the comparison of certain A. halleri and A. lyrata S-lineages with their A. thaliana orthologs.
evidence: This statement is supported by the discussion of previous studies.

claim: Some A. thaliana accessions with haplogroup A were able to reject A. halleri pollen expressing the cognate AhSCR04 specificity, despite about 6 million years of divergence.
source: Specifically, some A. thaliana accessions with haplogroup A were able to reject A. halleri pollen expressing the cognate AhSCR04 specificity (Tsuchimatsu et al., 2010), despite about 6 million years of divergence (Hohmann et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: An overexpressed version of A. thaliana SCR haplogroup C was able to elicit a SI reaction on pistils expressing the cognate A. lyrata AlSRK36 specificity.
source: Similarly, an overexpressed version of A. thaliana SCR haplogroup C was also able to elicit a SI reaction on pistils expressing the cognate A. lyrata AlSRK36 specificity (Dwyer et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to other scholarly work.

claim: A. thaliana has become predominantly self-fertilising, and no longer has an intact SI system due to alterations of SI components.
source: However, beside the fact that these were trans-specific comparisons, it is important to note that A. thaliana has become predominantly self-fertilising, and no longer has an intact SI system due to alterations of SI components (Bechsgaard et al., 2006; Shimizu and Tsuchimatsu, 2015), so our results provide the first direct test of the hypothesis that recognition specificities remain stable, rather than undergoing recurrent rapid turnover.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: The results provide the first direct test of the hypothesis that recognition specificities remain stable, rather than undergoing recurrent rapid turnover.
source: However, beside the fact that these were trans-specific comparisons, it is important to note that A. thaliana has become predominantly self-fertilising, and no longer has an intact SI system due to alterations of SI components (Bechsgaard et al., 2006; Shimizu and Tsuchimatsu, 2015), so our results provide the first direct test of the hypothesis that recognition specificities remain stable, rather than undergoing recurrent rapid turnover.
evidence: This is a statement about the significance of the study.

claim: The SI response elicited by the reconstructed SRKa was overall weaker and more variable across replicate lines than those elicited by the native SRK constructs.
source: Despite the obvious conservation of recognition specificity between SRKaIA and SRK03, we note that the SI response elicited by the reconstructed SRKa was overall weaker and more variable across replicate lines than those elicited by the native SRK constructs.
evidence: This is an observation based on the experimental data.

claim: The partial response could be due to incorrect inference of the ancestral receptor sequence.
source: This partial response could be due to incorrect inference of the ancestral receptor sequence.
evidence: This is a speculation about the cause of the partial response.

claim: Ancestral reconstruction is based on probabilistic inference, and a single amino acid modification (I vs M at position 208) can entirely compromise the SI response.
source: Ancestral reconstruction is based on probabilistic inference, and our results show that a single amino acid modification (I vs M at position 208) can entirely compromise the SI response.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing the effect of the amino acid at position 208.

claim: It is possible that the putative ancestral receptor had a partly diminished capacity to elicit the SI reaction because of imperfect reconstruction.
source: It is therefore possible that the putative ancestral receptor had a partly diminished capacity to elicit the SI reaction because of imperfect reconstruction.
evidence: This is a speculation about the cause of the partial response.

claim: The partial response could be due to parallel changes to the SCR ligand, followed by amino acid substitutions occurring between SRKa and SRK03 to fine-tune the SRK03/SCR03 interaction.
source: Alternatively, this partial response could be due to parallel changes to the SCR ligand, followed by amino acid substitutions occurring between SRKa and SRK03 to fine-tune the SRK03/SCR03 interaction.
evidence: This is a speculation about the cause of the partial response.

claim: Resurrection of the ancestral SCRa ligand will be needed to distinguish between the possibilities for the partial response.
source: Resurrection of the ancestral SCRa ligand will be needed to distinguish between these possibilities.
evidence: This is a statement about future work needed.

claim: Structural modelling of the cognate vs non-cognate complexes suggested that specificity of the receptor/ligand interaction depends on qualitative features rather than quantitative strength of the interaction.
source: Structural modelling of the cognate vs non-cognate complexes suggested that specificity of the receptor/ligand interaction depends on qualitative features rather than quantitative strength of the interaction.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural modeling analysis.

claim: A ligand is predicted to bind its non-cognate just as well as its cognate receptor, but it activates only the proper one by interacting with a different set of amino acid residues at the binding interface.
source: In other words, a ligand is predicted to bind its non-cognate just as well as its cognate receptor, but it activates only the proper one by interacting with a different set of amino acid residues at the binding interface.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural modeling analysis.

claim: This may point to a mechanism of allosteric activation, whereby changes in the set (rather than number) of amino acid contacts with the ligand lead to changes in the shape of the receptor.
source: This may point to a mechanism of allosteric activation, whereby changes in the set (rather than number) of amino acid contacts with the ligand lead to changes in the shape of the receptor.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism of specificity.

claim: Allosteric activation is important in the context of protein-protein interactions as well as of the binding of transcription factors to their DNA binding sites.
source: Allosteric activation is important in the context of protein-protein interactions (Kang et al., 2015) as well as of the binding of transcription factors to their DNA binding sites (Gronemeyer and Bourguet, 2009) and may be a general feature of molecular interfaces (Ma et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: The allosteric activation model suggests that only a few amino acid residues determine recognition specificity.
source: In our system, the allosteric activation model suggests that only a few amino acid residues determine recognition specificity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural modeling analysis.

claim: This can be tested by directly measuring binding affinities, following Ma et al. (2016).
source: This can be tested by directly measuring binding affinities, following Ma et al. (2016).
evidence: This is a statement about future work that can be done.

claim: It will be interesting to determine experimentally whether this conclusion extends to more diverged pairs of SCR-SRK alleles.
source: It will be interesting to determine experimentally whether this conclusion extends to more diverged pairs of SCR-SRK alleles, whose interactions are more common in SI systems than those between highly similar alleles studied here, because this balanced polymorphism has been maintained over a very long evolutionary time.
evidence: This is a statement about future work that can be done.

claim: Promoters of both SRK03 and SRK28 drive GFP expression specifically in stigmatic papillae cells.
source: Promoters of both SRK03 and SRK28 drive GFP expression specifically in stigmatic papillae cells (white arrows).
evidence: This is stated in the figure caption and supported by the microscopy images.

claim: SRK expression is located between stages 11 and 14, with a strong decrease of GFP fluorescence in mature flowers (old stage 15).
source: SRK expression is located between stages 11 and 14, with a strong decrease of GFP fluorescence in mature flowers (old stage 15).

source: No GFP signal was observed in any other part of the plant (inflorescence stems, leaves and non-reproductive floral organs, data not shown).
